title: TDDR Rising Narratives — Thursday evening, Nov 19
summary: A snapshot of opposition narratives from the Right and the Far Left as of 5:30 PM ET Thursday, Nov 19, 2026. Built for TDDR (Too Dumb Didn't Read). On the Far Left, the speaker fight moved from petitions to a nickname: 'AIPAC Shakur,' Charlamagne tha God's 2025 jab at Hakeem Jeffries, matched 5,557 posts in 24 hours (4.16× its prior average), the largest query tonight, while the Jeffries/AIPAC petition query fell to 2,095 (484 since 7 AM versus 2,782 the same hours Wednesday). On the Right, Rep. Lateefah Simon formally introduced the Protect Our Neighbors Act and the 'amnesty' frame surged: 4,118 posts (3.66×), 1,934 of them since 7 AM versus 20 the same hours Wednesday. New tonight: former Erie County Democratic chair Ian Murray, who learned from a passport review that he was never a U.S. citizen and left for Canada, became a noncitizen-voting talking point (1,259 posts, 1,126 since 7 AM versus 128); no coverage alleges he voted illegally. Also new: Jim Jordan's 'there'll be a third impeachment' warning (2,244 posts; 1,648 since 7 AM versus 501). Ron Johnson's Social Security 'Ponzi scheme' remark is cooling but still large (3,805 posts, 4.18×), the reparations card held steady (3,787), and popular-vote compact posts more than doubled in daytime hours. Two faded cards were dropped: the FAA/outage card and Bovino at Rutgers. Every count, quote, and fact-check comes from sources and X queries pulled this evening or carried over from this morning and labeled. Nothing here is invented.

trends.detail: U.S. trends were pulled at about 5:13 PM ET with x.get_trends_by_woeid (WOEID 23424977, max 50; 50 returned). Sports (Pete Rose, Puka, Ray Lewis, Goodell), a Cincinnati Zoo story ('Fiona,' 40,621 posts; 'Harambe'), tech (Anthropic, 152,613; WhatsApp, 135,639) and GTA dominated. 'Kasich' matches an X News story on John Kasich urging Republicans to drop MAGA after the midterms; it is an intra-GOP fight, not an opposition narrative, so we did not score it (the trend object carried no post count). 'Greenland' (26,208 posts) reflects Denmark's parliament ratifying the U.S.–Greenland defense pact, and 'Putin and Xi' is foreign news. None of the trends matched a scored query, so no card received the trend bonus this evening. Unlike this morning, many trend objects included tweet_count this time; where a trend had none, its volume is unavailable and we did not estimate it.

oppositionNote.body: Right = narratives the Right is pushing after the Democratic midterm wave. Far Left = pressure on Democratic leadership and the incoming majority from the party's left. Tonight the left's main target is still Jeffries, now through the 'AIPAC Shakur' nickname; Charlamagne tha God, who coined it, is not a party figure, but the card is tagged Far Left because that is where the attack lives. The Social Security card stays tagged Right because the 'Ponzi scheme' frame is a Right talking point, even though most posts matching it are backlash. The Erie and impeachment cards are tagged Right because their frames, 'noncitizens are running and voting' and 'they'll impeach instead of lowering costs,' are the Right's. The tag is the primary opposition frame.

methodology: Last updated Thursday, Nov 19, 2026, 5:30 PM ET. This is a research snapshot for TDDR, not a live API, and it will go stale overnight. U.S. X trends were pulled at about 5:13 PM ET. This morning's snapshot (Nov 19, 7:35 AM ET) is kept in the archive and was not overwritten. Thirteen of its fifteen narratives were re-counted with the same queries so momentum compares like with like. The new 24-hour window overlaps this morning's by 14 hours (5 PM Wednesday to 7 AM Thursday ET), so we also report each query's 7 AM–5 PM ET Thursday count against the same hours Wednesday. Two narratives were dropped because they faded: the FAA ground stop / cyberattack card (808 posts in the last 24 hours, 0.07× its prior daily average; 267 from 7 AM to 5 PM versus 1,240 the same hours Wednesday) and Bovino at Rutgers (482 posts, 0.16×). Three were added with new queries: 'AIPAC Shakur,' Ian Murray's citizenship case, and Jim Jordan's 'third impeachment' warning. One candidate was counted and not carved out as a card: Hasan Piker's argument that Democrats' large House margin weakens the left, which Neera Tanden and others criticized (516 posts, 1.00×; 333 from 7 AM to 5 PM versus 125 the same hours Wednesday), using a broader query than this morning's.

For each narrative we ran one English-language X search with x.get_posts_counts_recent at hourly granularity over a 167-hour window from 6:00 PM ET Thursday, Nov 12, through 5:00 PM ET Thursday, Nov 19. The last 24 hourly buckets (5:00 PM ET Wednesday, Nov 18, through 5:00 PM ET Thursday, Nov 19, exactly 24 hours) give the 24-hour count, and the whole window gives the 'seven-day' total. We counted named news or fact-check outlets whose coverage we opened or retrieved in this evening's searches and cite on the card. Official government pages, bill text, advocacy groups, research groups, pollsters, bill trackers, blogs, X News summaries, and X posts are cited as sources but not counted as outlets. We re-researched the immigration, Social Security and popular-vote compact cards, plus the three new cards, and counted only outlets retrieved this evening on those cards, which is why some outlet counts changed. We pulled a fresh post sample for the reparations card but no new coverage, so its outlet count is carried over. For the other cards, which we did not re-research this evening, the outlet count is carried over from this morning, and each of those cards says so. We noted whether each topic appeared on the U.S. trends list at about 5:13 PM ET.

Score = 50% volume index + 30% acceleration index + 20% coverage index. Volume index is 100 × log10(1 + last-24h posts) / log10(1 + the highest last-24h count in this set). Acceleration index is 100 × min(last-24h / prior daily average, 3) / 3, so a triple-or-higher average scores 100. Prior daily average is (seven-day total − last 24h) / 6. Coverage index is 70 × min(outlets, 7) / 7, plus 30 if the topic was on the U.S. X trends list this evening. No card got the trend bonus this evening. The Erie, 'AIPAC Shakur,' Social Security and immigration queries had low baselines earlier in the week, so their acceleration indices are maxed out. The impeachment and popular-vote queries carry last week's spikes in their seven-day totals, which keeps their acceleration low even though daytime volume rose. Read the post counts alongside the scores. Morning-to-evening score changes also reflect the lower volume ceiling (5,557 this evening versus 6,397 this morning) and how much coverage we retrieved.

Counts are query matches, not unique posts or unique users, and queries can overlap. The 'AIPAC Shakur,' Jeffries/AIPAC, Jeffries Iran funding, Jeffries ATM and DSA queries share many speaker-race posts. The Social Security query also catches posts attacking Johnson. The immigration query includes the phrase 'Stephen A' with Democrats/immigration terms, so it can catch unrelated Stephen A. Smith posts. The Erie query includes the bare word 'Erie' with citizenship or voting terms, so it can catch unrelated Erie posts, though our sample was all about Murray. The impeachment query needs an impeachment term, a Democratic/Jordan term and Trump or Hegseth, so it also catches Democrats discussing impeachment. The rigged-midterms query also catches posts mocking fraud claims. Replies are included, and automated @grok replies make up a visible share of several queries. Sentiment is a qualitative label from relevancy-sorted post samples and from quotes in news coverage, not a scientific poll. This evening we pulled fresh samples for the immigration, 'AIPAC Shakur,' Erie, impeachment, popular-vote compact, Social Security and reparations queries. Other cards carry this morning's sentiment and say so. Daily bar charts use UTC days (a UTC day starts at 7:00 PM ET the previous evening). Bars marked * are partial windows. Hourly charts are labeled in ET.

disinfo.caveatBody: New this evening: posts using the Ian Murray case as proof that noncitizens are voting have no evidence behind them; coverage says he believed he was a citizen through his mother, and none alleges he knowingly voted illegally. 'The Protect Our Neighbors Act gives 1.6 million people green cards' is misleading: the sponsor puts the number with final orders at about 1.19 million, orders would expire only after 10 years, a judge could renew them, and status is not automatic. 'Democrats are already preparing a third impeachment' is a prediction by Jim Jordan, not a report; Democratic leaders call impeachment an option, not a priority. 'Pro-Israel money delivered Jeffries's 251-11 win' remains unproven, since the ballot was secret. CNBC's experts say the 'Ponzi scheme' label misses how Social Security is funded; benefits would fall to about 78%, not zero, if the retirement fund is depleted in 2032. Carried over from this morning: PolitiFact has rated the Ponzi comparison False when others made it, and Johnson called his 'shut it down' line 'imprecise'; 'Pressley's H.R. 40 pays reparations' is misleading, since it creates a study commission; 'Democrats are importing voters' runs into the law, since noncitizens cannot vote in federal elections; 'Jeffries backs the Iran war' is false as stated; the '1.2 million signatures' figure against Jeffries remains unverified; 'Democrats will defund the military to shut down the government' is misleading; and Lead Stories found no '30,000-case' Texas voter fraud probe.

AARP's Bill Sweeney said Social Security 'runs on its own budget' and 'has never contributed a penny to the debt,' and CNBC notes the trustees project the retirement fund could be depleted in late 2032, when 78% of benefits would still be payable. CNBC also reports Johnson proposed a bill to fund retirement benefits from general revenue after depletion, which the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget said would 'absolutely explode the national debt.' Newsweek says Johnson is 'in hot water' over the remark. This morning's card (7:35 AM ET): Morning update (Nov 19): 6,397 posts in the last 24 hours, 28.84 times the prior daily average (last evening: 5,249 and 116.21×). From 5 PM ET Wednesday to 7 AM ET Thursday the query matched 2,227 posts, versus 1,077 in the same hours a night earlier. Overnight volume doubled the same hours a night earlier. New reporting this morning: Roll Call says Johnson told the hearing that if he has 'to pay a political price for that, I really don't care,' and notes the Social Security trustees project a 22% benefit cut by the end of 2032 without a fix. WPR reports Johnson's chairman's memo was titled 'Social Security: The Reality… a Legal Ponzi Scheme' and that nearly 1.4 million Wisconsinites get benefits. Newsweek quotes Maya MacGuineas of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget: 'It is not a Ponzi scheme.' Spectrum News says Johnson projects a $511 billion Social Security shortfall in 2032.
talkingPoints: Even the budget chairman admits it's a legal Ponzi scheme.
Social Security is a Ponzi scheme: today's workers pay today's retirees.
Young people will never see a dime of what they paid in.
It's not your money — Congress already spent it.
It's going broke by 2032 and nobody in Washington will say so.
Let workers invest in the market instead.
narratives.amplifiers: Right: @SenRonJohnson and his hearing memo; reposts from The Post Millennial (@TPostMillennial), Just the News and Fox News. Backlash: Sen. Ron Wyden (quoted by CNBC), AARP, the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, and accounts such as @Patrickwebb (246 likes, 5,284 views) and @JohnWKraus.
narratives.whyItWorks: 'Ponzi scheme' is a sticky, intuitive metaphor for a pay-as-you-go system, and genuine insolvency projections give it a factual hook. It speaks to young workers' fear that they pay in and get nothing, and it moves the debate from 'how to fix' to 'whether to keep.' For Democrats, the 'shut it down' quote is a gift, which is why the backlash outran the original.
narratives.audience: Libertarian and fiscal-conservative voters, younger right-leaning men skeptical of entitlements, and Fox Business/Newsmax audiences. The backlash reaches seniors, Wisconsin voters and the broad Democratic base.
narratives.counter: Use his own walk-back: even Johnson now says he isn't proposing to shut it down. Then explain the difference: a Ponzi scheme is a fraud that hides how it works; Social Security is a public, legally mandated program that can be kept solvent by changing taxes or benefits (PolitiFact). Name the fix: lifting the payroll tax cap ($184,500 in 2026, per The Hill) closes much of the gap without cutting benefits.

factChecks.claim: Social Security adds to the national debt like a Ponzi scheme that will collapse.
factChecks.detail: CNBC quotes AARP that Social Security runs on its own dedicated budget and cannot borrow; CBO notes its shortfalls do affect the unified deficit when outlays exceed dedicated revenue. The trustees project the retirement trust fund could be depleted in the fourth quarter of 2032, after which about 78% of scheduled benefits would still be payable, not zero. This is TDDR's read of CNBC's reporting, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

factChecks.claim: Social Security is a Ponzi scheme.
factChecks.detail: PolitiFact rated Rick Perry's Ponzi comparison False in 2011 and, reviewing the same claim from Elon Musk in 2025, said that unlike a Ponzi scheme Social Security is transparent, has oversight, promises no unrealistic returns, and can be made solvent through changes to taxes or benefits. It also noted the superficial similarity: current workers' taxes pay current retirees. PolitiFact has not rated Johnson's Nov. 18 remark.

factChecks.claim: Sen. Ron Johnson wants to shut down Social Security.
factChecks.rating: He said it, then retracted it
factChecks.detail: On Fox Business he said 'you just shut it down.' Hours later, at his own hearing, he called that 'imprecise' and said he is 'not proposing shutting down Social Security' (The Hill). He has long proposed making Social Security discretionary spending, subject to annual appropriations (HuffPost). This is TDDR's read of that reporting, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

narratives.sentimentNote: In a relevancy sample of posts from 7 AM to 5 PM ET Thursday, nearly every post was about the bill rather than Stephen A. Smith. Most called it amnesty or a reward for 'ignoring court orders': @ElectionWiz ('AMNESTY UPDATE,' 172 likes, 19,758 views, the most-viewed post we saw), @RedWavePress ('DISGUSTING… WIPE OUT deportation orders,' 4,388 views) and @Bubblebathgirl (3,386 views). A second cluster quoted Stephen A. Smith that Democrats use immigration to dilute the Black vote, some adding 'Black Americans are being replaced'; others called him 'an idiot' and noted Republicans benefited from Cuban migration. From 7 AM to 5 PM ET Thursday the query matched 1,934 posts, versus 20 in the same hours Wednesday. The bill was formally introduced Thursday by Rep. Lateefah Simon with Reps. John Garamendi, Zoe Lofgren and Juan Vargas (Simon's office; SFGate), and the daytime count jumped: 1,934 posts from 7 AM to 5 PM ET versus 20 in the same hours Wednesday. Simon's office puts the number of people living with final removal orders at about 1.19 million, lower than the 1.6 million figure from ICE testimony that most posts repeat. The bill text lets an order expire 10 years after it was issued; a judge can renew it on 'clear and convincing evidence,' and a person can then petition for status only after 10 years of continuous presence and no conviction for a crime punishable by more than a year. Stephen A. Smith's barbershop remarks stayed in the conversation through coverage such as The Comeback ('same arrogance from Democratic Party'), but in our sample the bill drove the volume. Republicans control the House until January, so the bill has no path this session. This morning's card (7:35 AM ET): New this morning. The query matched 2,208 posts in the last 24 hours (1.88× its prior daily average), and 2,188 of them came from 5 PM ET Wednesday to 7 AM ET Thursday, versus 17 in the same hours a night earlier. It combines two threads. First, Rep. Lateefah Simon (D-Calif.) is introducing the Protect Our Neighbors Act on Thursday: final removal orders would expire after 10 years for people continuously present in the U.S. with no criminal conviction, and those people could seek a green card. A judge could renew an order on 'clear and convincing evidence' (ABC News). Former acting ICE Director Todd Lyons told lawmakers there are about 1.6 million people with final orders, but not all would qualify, and ABC says the bill is unlikely to move before January. Second, X News summarized a barbershop conversation in which Stephen A. Smith, now registered independent, argued that Democrats' immigration policies build a Latino voting bloc and reduce reliance on Black voters, a point he has made before on SiriusXM (Yahoo Sports quoted him calling open borders 'a direct assault against Black voters'). Roland Martin called the argument nonsensical, per X News. An earlier spike on Nov. 13 (5,100 posts that UTC day) came from coverage of President Trump's interview with Smith, in which Trump said immigration reform is 'possible' (USA Today); that spike raises the prior daily average, which is why acceleration is only 1.88×. A narrower count of only the bill (its name, Rep. Simon, or 'deportation orders expire') found 281 posts, 274 of them overnight, so most of this query's volume came from the Smith clip.

Ignore a judge for 10 years and get a green card.
Democrats just filed amnesty: ignore a deportation order for 10 years and you get a green card.
1.6 million deportation orders would be wiped out.
Democrats bring in migrants to replace Black voters.
They ran on affordability, and the first bill is for illegal immigrants.

narratives.whyItWorks: 'Amnesty' and 'expiration date' turn a narrow, conditional bill into a simple story about rewarding people who ignored a judge, and the bill's formal introduction gave the Right a fresh news peg on day one of the 'affordability' majority. The large, unexplained '1.6 million' number makes it sound sweeping. The Smith clip adds a Black, non-Republican messenger to a replacement frame the Right has used for years.

narratives.counter: Read the bill's limits aloud: an order has to be 10 years old, the person needs 10 years of continuous presence and no serious conviction, and a judge can renew the order (bill text; ABC News). Use the sponsor's own number, about 1.19 million people with final orders, and say plainly that only some would qualify. Name who it was written for: a 73-year-old grandmother who checked in with ICE for 30 years. On 'importing voters': a green card is not citizenship, and noncitizens cannot vote in federal elections (18 U.S.C. § 611).

It does not hand out green cards automatically, and it has no path in the current Republican House. This is TDDR's read of the bill text and Simon's release, not a rating from a fact-check outlet.

factChecks.detail: About 1.6 million people have final removal orders (ICE testimony cited by ABC News), but the bill covers only orders at least 10 years old for people continuously present with no criminal conviction, and a judge could renew an order. narratives.sentimentNote: In a relevancy sample of posts from 7 AM to 5 PM ET Thursday, the biggest post by far was @ScottPresler ('You can't make this up. -1 in PA,' 3,430 likes, 1,153 reposts, 35,777 views). @TonySeruga's 'Former Democrat Leader Flees to Canada' had 4,468 views. narratives.summary: New this evening. The query matched 1,259 posts in the last 24 hours (40.18× its prior daily average); 1,126 of them came from 7 AM to 5 PM ET Thursday, versus 128 in the same hours Wednesday. The Erie Times-News reported Wednesday that Ian Murray, 75, who chaired the Erie County Democratic Party from 1986 to 1998 and sat on the Democratic National Committee, left for Nova Scotia on Nov. 12 after the government determined he was never a U.S. citizen. He was born in Canada in 1951 and moved to Erie at 5. He believed he was a citizen through his mother, but under the Nationality Act of 1940 her U.S. residence fell just short of 10 years because her semesters at the University of Toronto did not count. A first-ever passport application about 18 months ago set off the review; an immigration judge granted voluntary departure (Erie Times-News; WJET/YourErie; The Center Square). The Right turned it into proof that noncitizens hold office and vote. None of the coverage we retrieved alleges or documents that he knowingly voted illegally, and he had retired from politics and was living in Maine.
talkingPoints: A DNC member and county Democratic chair was never a citizen. How many more are there?
If he got through, noncitizens are on the voter rolls everywhere.
This is why we need proof of citizenship to vote (the SAVE Act).
Democrats say noncitizen voting is a myth. Tell that to Ian Murray.
narratives.amplifiers: Right: @ScottPresler (3,430 likes, 35,777 views), @TonySeruga (4,468 views), Dean Cain, Libs of TikTok (whose post drew many @grok fact-check replies), and sites such as Gateway Pundit, WLT Report and Blabber Buzz. Local reporting: the Erie Times-News (Ed Palattella) and WJET.
narratives.whyItWorks: It's a real, verifiable story with an irresistible headline: a Democratic Party boss turns out to be a noncitizen and 'flees to Canada.' It lets the Right make an abstract claim (noncitizens vote) concrete with one face, and the technical cause, a 1940 law and a mother's college semesters, is too complicated to fit in a reply.
narratives.audience: Election-integrity activists, SAVE Act supporters, Pennsylvania Republicans, and X audiences who already believe noncitizen voting is widespread.
narratives.counter: Agree on the facts, then shrink the claim: this is one man who believed for 70 years that he was a citizen through his mother, and the system caught it when he applied for a passport (Erie Times-News). No coverage alleges he knowingly voted illegally. PolitiFact has found noncitizen voting rare, and Pennsylvania voters must attest to citizenship under penalty of law when they register. narratives.whyItWorks: Affordability won Democrats the midterms, so 'they'll raise your taxes' attacks the brand at its strongest point. It's also partly true — Democrats are debating tax increases — which makes the exaggeration ('on Americans') harder to rebut in one line.
